label: pathway significance needs a null model
text: PITFALL: 'Significantly mutated pathway' is a statistical claim, so reporting a raw percent of samples with any pathway mutation does not settle it; large pathways (ERBB/PI3K/RTK gene sets with dozens of long genes) will be hit in many samples by chance alone. CHECK: compute the number of samples with >=1 nonsilent mutation in the pathway genes and compare to a null that accounts for each sample's mutation count and gene coding length (e.g. permute mutations per sample over genes weighted by CDS length, or PathScan-style per-sample binomial combined by Fisher). IF FOUND: base the True/False call on the null-model p-value, not the raw frequency; a high raw frequency with p>0.05 does not contradict 'not significantly mutated'. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3106187/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6892778/

label: pathway gene-set definition
text: PITFALL: The result depends heavily on which genes define 'ERBB-PI3K' (narrow ERBB1-4+PIK3CA/PIK3R1/PTEN/AKT/MTOR/TSC vs. broad KEGG RTK-RAS-PI3K sets of ~100 genes). CHECK: state the gene list explicitly; run the test with a narrow curated set (Sanchez-Vega 2018 TCGA PI3K + ERBB receptors: EGFR, ERBB2, ERBB3, ERBB4, PIK3CA, PIK3CB, PIK3R1, PIK3R2, PTEN, AKT1-3, MTOR, TSC1, TSC2, RICTOR, RPTOR, STK11, INPP4B, PPP2R1A) and a broader KEGG ErbB set, and see if the conclusion changes. IF FOUND: if conclusions differ, report the curated-set result as primary and note sensitivity. SOURCE: https://gdc.cancer.gov/about-data/publications/Pathways-2018 ; https://mskcc-epi-bio.github.io/gnomeR/reference/pathways.html

label: nonsilent only
text: PITFALL: Counting silent, intronic, UTR, flank or non-coding variants as pathway mutations inflates pathway hits; driver/pathway tests count nonsilent coding mutations and use silent ones only for the background rate. CHECK: tabulate Variant_Classification in data_mutations.txt; restrict pathway hits to Missense, Nonsense, Frame_Shift, In_Frame, Splice_Site, Translation_Start_Site, Nonstop. IF FOUND: rerun with nonsilent-only; optionally use silent counts to estimate background rate. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3769934/ ; https://www.genepattern.org/modules/docs/MutSigCV/1/

label: germline/common variant filtering
text: PITFALL: This MAF has a FILTER column (values like 'common_variant') and ExAC_AF/GMAF population-frequency columns; residual germline polymorphisms (especially in Asian-ancestry cohorts poorly represented in references) can create spurious recurrent 'mutations' in pathway genes. CHECK: count pathway-gene variants with FILTER != PASS/'.' or ExAC_AF/ExAC_AF_EAS > 0.01, and variants recurring at identical positions in many samples without known hotspot status. IF FOUND: exclude common_variant / population AF>1% calls and rerun the pathway test. SOURCE: https://townsend-lab-yale.github.io/cancereffectsizeR/articles/MAF_filtering_tips.html ; https://doi.org/10.1186/s12920-017-0296-8

label: sample ID mismatch / denominator
text: PITFALL: Sample identifiers may not match between tables (clinical uses e.g. 'NPC15F' while the MAF Tumor_Sample_Barcode uses e.g. 'NPC015D'), so a naive join can drop samples or mis-set the denominator. CHECK: compare the set of Tumor_Sample_Barcode values to SAMPLE_ID in data_clinical_sample.txt, and note how many sequenced samples have zero mutations. IF FOUND: use the clinical sample count (all sequenced NPC samples) as the denominator, normalising ID formats if needed; never use only samples present in the MAF as the denominator without checking. SOURCE: https://townsend-lab-yale.github.io/cancereffectsizeR/articles/MAF_filtering_tips.html

label: hypermutator outliers
text: PITFALL: One or a few hypermutated tumours can carry most pathway mutations and make a pathway look significantly mutated. CHECK: look at TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS / mutations per sample; check what fraction of pathway hits come from the top 1-3 samples. IF FOUND: use a per-sample null (expected hits scale with each sample's mutation count) or report results with hypermutators excluded; count samples mutated, not total mutations. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8406556/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6892778/

label: one sample per patient
text: PITFALL: If a cohort has multiple samples per patient (e.g. primary plus recurrence, or multi-region), counting each sample separately inflates recurrence. CHECK: compare unique PATIENT_ID vs SAMPLE_ID counts and look for suffixes (e.g. trailing letters) that may mark repeat samples. IF FOUND: collapse to one sample per patient before computing pathway frequency/significance. SOURCE: https://townsend-lab-yale.github.io/cancereffectsizeR/articles/MAF_filtering_tips.html

label: multiple testing
text: PITFALL: When several pathways or gene sets are tested, unadjusted p-values overstate significance, and Fisher-combined p-values are anti-conservative when inputs are correlated. CHECK: record how many pathway/gene-set tests were run. IF FOUND: apply Benjamini-Hochberg across the pathways tested and treat the ERBB-PI3K result as significant only if q<0.05 (or p<0.05 if it is the single pre-specified test). label: Fusion status vs histology
text: PITFALL: Fusion status (FP vs FN-RMS) is not the same as histology; ~20-25% of alveolar RMS are PAX-FOXO1 fusion-negative and behave like embryonal RMS, so grouping by ONCOTREE_CODE ARMS/ERMS misclassifies patients. CHECK: In data_sv.txt look for PAX3-FOXO1 or PAX7-FOXO1 (Site1/Site2_Hugo_Symbol PAX3/PAX7 with FOXO1) per patient, and check whether any clinical column states fusion status; cross-tab against ONCOTREE_CODE. IF FOUND: Define FP vs FN from detected fusions (any sample of the patient), not from histology; report how many ARMS lack a fusion. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6637949/

label: Acquired = paired within-patient
text: PITFALL: 'Acquire new alterations' is a within-patient longitudinal claim; comparing pooled alteration counts across all samples (or TMB per sample) between FP and FN groups does not measure acquisition. CHECK: Identify patients with >=2 samples (PATIENT_ID repeated in data_clinical_sample.txt; SAMPLE_TYPE Primary vs Local Recurrence/Metastasis, sample suffix T01,T02..), order them, and for each patient count alterations (mutations, CNA, SV) present in later sample but absent in the earliest. IF FOUND: Compare the per-patient number of acquired alterations between FN and FP patients (one value per patient, e.g. Mann-Whitney or descriptive given small n), not per-sample counts. SOURCE: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-025-02204-3

label: Panel version mismatch in pairs
text: PITFALL: Paired samples from the same patient were often sequenced on different MSK-IMPACT panel versions (IMPACT341/410/468/505), so a gene 'gained' in the later sample may simply not have been covered in the earlier one, inflating acquired-alteration counts. CHECK: Use data_gene_panel_matrix.txt to get each sample's panel; for every apparent new alteration verify the gene is on the earlier sample's panel. IF FOUND: Restrict acquired/lost comparisons to genes covered by both panels of the pair (intersection); for TMB compare per-Mb values not raw counts. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7174078/

label: Purity-driven false private calls
text: PITFALL: Low tumour purity in one sample of a pair causes false-negative mutation and CNA calls, making alterations look 'acquired' (or lost) when they were merely undetected; CNAs especially go flat at low purity. CHECK: Compare TUMOR_PURITY and SAMPLE_COVERAGE between the two samples of each pair; check VAF (t_alt_count/(t_alt_count+t_ref_count)) of 'private' mutations and whether their sample had purity <=30%. IF FOUND: Flag or exclude pairs with low-purity samples, report results with and without them, and treat private low-VAF calls cautiously. SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5015593/

label: MSI confounding and NA MSI status

label: mCRC subset and sidedness definition
text: PITFALL: The hypothesis is about metastatic CRC (mCRC), but the cohort includes MCRC_TYPE='Early Stage Primary' samples (~123) and 14 samples with PRIMARY_TUMOR_LOCATION=NA. label: Per-gene testing and multiplicity
text: PITFALL: The hypothesis lists six genes; judging it on one pooled 'any of six altered' test or on one gene alone can mislead, and testing six genes without correction overstates significance. Known biology in MSS mCRC: right-sided enriched for BRAF V600E, KRAS, PIK3CA, often SMAD4/RNF43/AKT1 small numbers; left-sided enriched for APC/TP53. reason: TMB can confound KIT enrichment differently in different subtypes. Separating driver from passenger KIT calls changes how the result should be read.
text: Melanoma is UV-hypermutated, so many KIT calls are passenger mutations whose rate follows TMB. Driver KIT mutations cluster in hotspots: exon 11 (e.g. V559, L576P), exon 13 (K642E), exon 17 (D816, N822) and exon 9. Report two frequencies per subtype: any non-silent KIT, and KIT hotspot/driver. Compare TMB between subtypes. If TMB differs, also run a logistic regression of KIT status on subtype adjusted for log TMB.

reason: The choice of test and the reading of the result matter when counts are this sparse.

With small counts, a non-significant result means low power.

Count the patients who have PROGNOSTIC_MODEL, IPI and OS all present, and compare the genomic model with IPI head to head on them. Testing single genes against survival does not answer the question.

reason: This sets the criterion that decides the label. P-value comparisons are the most likely error.
text: To show 'outperforms', it is not enough for both predictors to be significant on log-rank, or for one to have a smaller p-value. Fit Cox models OS~IPI, OS~genomic model and OS~IPI+genomic model on the same patients. Compare discrimination (Harrell's C) and AIC, and run likelihood-ratio tests of the combined model against each single model. Outperformance means a clearly higher C for the genomic model, with a paired CI for the difference that excludes 0. Adding information beyond IPI (significant LRT) is a weaker claim and should be reported as such.

reason: Unpaired comparisons on different subsets give results that cannot be interpreted.
text: IPI and PROGNOSTIC_MODEL are missing for different patients. Compute every comparison on the intersection of patients with both predictors and valid OS. Get a paired CI for the difference in C by bootstrap, or with survival::concordance on both fits together. A C-index or p-value from different patient sets cannot be compared.

reason: Overfitting bias can make the genomic model look better than it is.
text: The genomic risk model was probably derived from this same cohort, so its performance here is in-sample and optimistic. IPI was defined externally. Check the column descriptions for training/validation information or a cohort split column. Treat a small in-sample advantage for the genomic model (C difference under about 0.03) as weak evidence. If you build your own gene-based model, use bootstrap optimism correction (at least 100 resamples, redoing selection each time) or cross-validation.

reason: Mishandling the comparator variable biases the head-to-head comparison.
text: The IPI column can be missing or inconsistent even when its factor columns exist. Recompute IPI as the sum of the five 0/1 factors and check it against the IPI column. reason: If the event coding is wrong, every survival result is wrong.

text: Both predictors are coarse ordinal scores (3 genomic groups against 6 IPI levels), so many risk scores are tied. Score ties as 0.5 in Harrell's C, which is the survival::concordance default. reason: Tells the team which kind of evidence the data can and cannot provide before they build an analysis around VAF.
text: Clonal selection means a shift in clone frequency (cellular prevalence), which normally needs allele read counts plus copy number and purity. The library reports that t_ref_count and t_alt_count in data_mutations.txt are empty for all rows; check this by counting non-empty values. If they are empty, do not claim that VAFs or prevalences rose or fell. Use what remains (mutations present in one sample and absent in another, and the copy-number tables) and say how much weaker that evidence is.

reason: Defines the right comparison unit. Mixing in later passages or xenograft-only patients would test a different claim.
text: The hypothesis is about INITIAL engraftment, meaning patient tumour (T) to the first xenograft passage. List the patients that have both a T sample and an early X sample (X0/X1 or the earliest available) on the same platform. Some patients (e.g. SA429, SA496) reportedly have xenograft samples only. Keep changes at later passages separate, because they answer a different question. Look for any variable that marks primary versus metastatic origin. If none exists, say so and judge the general claim on the pairs you have.

reason: Without this check the team could misread an artefact of table structure as evidence against selection.
text: In data_mutations.txt, the targeted-sequencing samples of a patient may all have the same number of rows (e.g. 184 for every SA501 targeted sample, 144 for every SA532). If so, those rows are a list of genotyped sites, not of sites detected in each sample. Per patient, compare the (Chromosome, Start_Position, Alt) sets across the targeted samples. If the sets are identical, the targeted rows carry no presence/absence information. Base any mutation-level T-versus-X comparison on the whole_genome samples, and do not read identical targeted sets as 'no selection'.

reason: This artefact pushes the result directly toward apparent selection, so the team must control for it.
text: Mouse DNA in xenograft samples can produce false-positive SNVs that appear only in the xenograft and look like newly emerging clones. Check whether xenograft-private mutations are mostly noncoding or silent, scattered and non-recurrent, or rising with passage number. Also look for whole_genome samples with extreme call counts (e.g. SA531X1). If you see these signs, discount xenograft-only mutations and give more weight to mutations lost from the tumour, or to segment-level copy-number changes, because contamination cannot create losses.

reason: Private-mutation counts are the obvious metric and are confounded by sensitivity.
text: Mutations private to the T or the X WGS sample can come from differences in detection sensitivity (depth, purity, low-VAF variants) rather than real clonal gain or loss. WGS call counts reportedly vary a lot within a patient (e.g. SA531T about 481 versus SA531X1 about 1,514). For each T/X pair, compare total counts and private fractions, and check whether the excess of private calls simply tracks one sample's total. Do not count every private mutation as selection. Require a consistent pattern across patients, recognisable cancer genes, or supporting copy-number evidence.

reason: Differences in calling pipeline between T and X can create spurious T/X differences.

reason: This sets the evidence standard for the label. Without it, a team could read a high raw mutation frequency as significance.
text: Whether a pathway is 'significantly mutated' is a statistical question. The percent of samples with any pathway mutation does not answer it, because large gene sets made of long genes get hit by chance. Count the samples with at least one nonsilent mutation in the pathway genes and compare that count with a null model that accounts for each sample's mutation count and each gene's coding length (for example, permute each sample's mutations across genes weighted by CDS length, or run per-sample binomial tests and combine them PathScan-style). Make the call from the null-model p-value. A high raw frequency with p>0.05 does not contradict 'not significantly mutated'.

reason: How the gene set is defined can flip the conclusion, so it needs to be fixed in advance and checked for sensitivity.
text: The result depends heavily on which genes define ERBB-PI3K. Write the gene list out. Use a narrow curated set as the primary test: EGFR, ERBB2, ERBB3, ERBB4, PIK3CA, PIK3CB, PIK3R1, PIK3R2, PTEN, AKT1, AKT2, AKT3, MTOR, TSC1, TSC2, RICTOR, RPTOR, STK11, INPP4B and PPP2R1A, which is the TCGA 2018 PI3K set plus the ERBB receptors. Then rerun with a broader KEGG ErbB set as a sensitivity check. If the two disagree, report the curated result as primary and note the difference.

reason: Including non-coding or silent variants inflates the number of pathway hits.
text: Count only nonsilent coding variants as pathway hits: Missense, Nonsense, Frame_Shift, In_Frame, Splice_Site, Translation_Start_Site and Nonstop (check the Variant_Classification column in data_mutations.txt). Leave out silent, intronic, UTR, flank and other non-coding variants. Silent variants can be used to estimate the background rate.

reason: The hypothesis is restricted to MSS; the MSS definition and NA handling directly change the analysed cohort and can create spurious enrichment.
text: MSI-high colorectal tumours are mostly right-sided and carry BRAF V600E and RNF43 frameshifts (e.g. G659fs), so including them can make BRAF/RNF43 look right-enriched through MSI confounding alone. Tabulate MSI_STATUS (MSS/MSI/Inconclusive/NA) by PRIMARY_TUMOR_LOCATION in data_clinical_sample.txt and analyse MSS only. Many samples (about 327) have MSI_STATUS=NA but an MSI_SCORE; decide explicitly how to handle them (e.g. MSIsensor cut-offs: <3 MSS, 3-10 indeterminate, >=10 MSI-H) and report results both for strict MSI_STATUS==MSS and for score-derived MSS.

reason: Germline artefacts can make the pathway look falsely significant.
text: data_mutations.txt has a FILTER column (with values such as 'common_variant') and population-frequency columns (ExAC_AF, GMAF). Leftover germline polymorphisms, which are common in Asian-ancestry cohorts that reference panels cover poorly, can look like recurrent pathway mutations. Exclude calls flagged common_variant and calls with population AF above 1% (including ExAC_AF_EAS). Be wary of variants that recur at the same position in many samples but are not known hotspots. Rerun the test after filtering.

reason: Defines the correct population (metastatic) and the exposure variable (sidedness); both are easy to get wrong.
text: The hypothesis concerns metastatic CRC, but the cohort includes MCRC_TYPE='Early Stage Primary' samples (about 123) and about 14 samples with PRIMARY_TUMOR_LOCATION=NA. Tabulate MCRC_TYPE and PRIMARY_TUMOR_LOCATION; run the main analysis on mCRC samples (mCRC Primary + mCRC Metastasis) with known Left/Right side, and include early-stage samples only as a sensitivity analysis. Standard convention: right = caecum to transverse colon (proximal to splenic flexure), left = splenic flexure to rectum. Check PRIMARY_SITE against the provided Right/Left label; transverse colon handling varies and rectum may behave differently from left colon.

reason: A naive join drops samples and changes the denominator for frequency and significance.
text: Sample IDs do not match between tables: the clinical table uses IDs like 'NPC15F' while Tumor_Sample_Barcode in the MAF uses IDs like 'NPC015D'. Compare the two ID sets and normalise the formats. Use all sequenced samples in data_clinical_sample.txt as the denominator, including any with zero mutations, not only the samples that appear in the MAF.

reason: Duplicate patients double-count and break independence in Fisher tests.
text: About 31 patients have more than one sequenced sample (e.g. primary and metastasis). Count SAMPLE_ID per PATIENT_ID among MSS samples with known side and collapse to one row per patient before testing (either altered-if-any-sample-altered, or one prespecified sample such as the primary). Primary-metastasis concordance is high for KRAS/BRAF but lower for PIK3CA, so state the rule used.

reason: Counting repeat samples from the same patient inflates recurrence.
text: Check whether any patient has more than one sample (compare unique PATIENT_ID with SAMPLE_ID, and look for suffixes that mark repeat samples). If so, keep one sample per patient before testing the pathway.

reason: If panel mix differs by side, uncovered genes counted as wild-type bias the side comparison.
text: Samples were sequenced on different MSK-IMPACT panels (IMPACT341/410/468). Genes added in later panels (RNF43 may be absent from IMPACT341 - verify in data_gene_panel_matrix.txt / panel gene lists, and check whether any RNF43 mutation occurs in IMPACT341 samples) would be wrongly counted as wild-type in samples whose panel did not cover them. Cross-tabulate panel by side, and compute each gene's frequency with a denominator restricted to samples whose panel covers that gene; also exclude samples with mutations=NA in the panel matrix.

label: CALR in JAK2-wt MPN
text: In this MPN study (151 samples, all tumor-normal matched), 25 of 39 JAK2-nonmutated samples carry somatic CALR exon 9 frameshifts (L367Tfs*46 type 1, K385Nfs*47 type 2), and no CALR mutation co-occurs with JAK2 mutation.

reason: Hypermutators can drive a false significant result.
text: One or a few hypermutated tumours can carry most of the pathway mutations. Look at mutations per sample (and TMB if it is available) and at what share of pathway hits comes from the top 1-3 samples. Count samples mutated rather than total mutations, use a per-sample null, or report the result with hypermutators excluded.

reason: The alteration definition determines the counts; counting VUS/passengers inflates frequencies, and CNA data are needed for SMAD4.
text: The hypothesis is about ONCOGENIC alterations, and the mutation file has no OncoKB/oncogenic annotation column. List Variant_Classification and protein changes for KRAS, BRAF, PIK3CA, AKT1, RNF43, SMAD4, and define 'oncogenic' a priori before testing, e.g. KRAS G12/G13/Q61/K117/A146; BRAF V600 and class 2/3 kinase-domain variants; PIK3CA hotspots (E542/E545/H1047 etc.); AKT1 E17K; truncating mutations in RNF43 and SMAD4, plus SMAD4 deep deletions (value -2) from data_cna.txt. Report results under both an 'any non-synonymous' and a 'hotspot/truncating' definition and check whether the conclusion holds under both. Exclude silent/intronic rows.

reason: This prevents a wrong 'Not verifiable' call and stops teams comparing these data with published rates that include copy-number alterations.
text: The only molecular data here are point mutations and indels; there is no copy-number file. Published ERBB-PI3K alteration rates often include amplifications, which these data cannot show. Frame the test as mutation-level significance. Mutation data are enough to test 'significantly mutated', so a missing CNA file is not by itself grounds for 'Not verifiable'.

reason: A few hypermutators can drive apparent side differences within the MSS group.
text: Hypermutated MSS tumours (e.g. POLE exonuclease-domain mutants, aa 268-471; TMB often >50 mut/Mb) carry many incidental mutations in KRAS/BRAF/PIK3CA etc. and can inflate frequencies on whichever side they fall. Inspect TMB_NONSYNONYMOUS among MSS samples, POLE exonuclease mutations, and MSI_SCORE values in the 3-10 range, and run a sensitivity analysis excluding hypermutated MSS samples (e.g. TMB>20).

reason: Unadjusted multiple tests overstate significance.
text: Record how many pathway or gene-set tests you run. If you test several, apply Benjamini-Hochberg and treat ERBB-PI3K as significant only if q<0.05. If it is the single pre-specified test, use p<0.05. Fisher-combined p-values are anti-conservative when their inputs are correlated.

reason: Gives a prespecified multi-gene decision rule and multiple-testing control, so the label is not driven by one gene or by uncorrected p-values.
text: The hypothesis names six genes. Do not judge it on a single pooled 'any of six altered' test or on one gene alone. Run per-gene 2x2 Fisher tests (right vs left, MSS, one row per patient, panel-aware denominators), report odds ratios with 95% CI, direction of each effect, and Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted q-values. Decide in advance how the per-gene results map to a label: consider how many genes show right-side enrichment, whether the main ones are significant after FDR correction, and whether any gene is significantly enriched in the opposite direction. Rare genes (e.g. AKT1) may be underpowered; an underpowered non-significant result is not by itself a contradiction.

reason: This defines the right unit of analysis. A pooled per-sample comparison answers a different question and could give the wrong label.
text: 'Acquiring new alterations' is a within-patient, over-time claim. Find patients with two or more samples (repeated PATIENT_ID in data_clinical_sample.txt; use SAMPLE_TYPE such as Primary vs Recurrence/Metastasis, or sample suffixes T01/T02, to put them in order). For each patient, count alterations present in a later sample but absent from the earliest one. Then compare these per-patient acquired counts between fusion-negative (FN) and fusion-positive (FP) patients. Pooled per-sample alteration counts or TMB do not measure acquisition.

reason: Grouping by histology would put some patients in the wrong group, and that would change the FN vs FP comparison.
text: Define FP vs FN-RMS by whether a PAX3-FOXO1 or PAX7-FOXO1 fusion is detected in data_sv.txt (Site1/Site2_Hugo_Symbol), in any sample of the patient, or by an explicit fusion-status clinical column if one exists. Do not define it by histology (ONCOTREE_CODE ARMS vs ERMS): about 20-25% of alveolar RMS are fusion-negative. Cross-tabulate fusion status against histology and report it.

reason: Tumours mainly gain copy-number changes during progression, so counting mutations alone could reverse the conclusion.
text: 'Alterations' includes more than SNVs/indels. Tally acquired events separately for mutations (data_mutations.txt), discrete CNAs (data_cna.txt values of +2/-2) and SVs (data_sv.txt). You can also compare fraction genome altered from data_cna_hg19.seg. State whether any FN vs FP difference holds for each alteration type.

reason: Differences in panel coverage can create false 'new' alterations and inflate one group's acquired count.
text: Samples from the same patient may have been sequenced on different MSK-IMPACT panel versions (IMPACT341/410/468/505; see data_gene_panel_matrix.txt). A gene 'gained' in the later sample may simply not have been on the earlier sample's panel. Count acquired or lost alterations only in genes covered by both panels of the pair. For TMB, compare per-Mb values.

reason: This artefact directly inflates or deflates per-patient acquired counts.
text: Low tumour purity in one sample of a pair causes missed mutation and CNA calls, so alterations look acquired or lost when they were just undetected. Compare TUMOR_PURITY and SAMPLE_COVERAGE within each pair, and check the VAF of private mutations. Report results with and without pairs that include a sample of purity <=30%.

text: PLAN: Quantity = number of NPC samples (one per patient, all clinical samples as denominator) with >=1 nonsilent mutation in curated ERBB-PI3K set (EGFR ERBB2-4 PIK3CA PIK3CB PIK3R1 PIK3R2 PTEN AKT1-3 MTOR TSC1 TSC2 RICTOR RPTOR STK11 INPP4B PPP2R1A). Method: filter common_variant/pop AF>1%, then permutation null placing each sample's nonsilent mutations across genes weighted by CDS length (approximated by protein length from MAF); p<0.05 single pre-specified test. Checks: ID normalisation, duplicates per patient, hypermutators, recurrent non-hotspot positions, KEGG ErbB sensitivity. Change method if hypermutators dominate (then exclude) or filtering changes counts drastically.

label: PLAN
text: PLAN: Estimate per-gene right vs left alteration frequency (KRAS,BRAF,PIK3CA,AKT1,RNF43,SMAD4) in MSS mCRC (mCRC Primary+Metastasis, known side), one row per patient (altered if any sample), panel-aware denominators. Fisher tests with OR, 95% CI, BH q. Two definitions: any non-synonymous, and hotspot/truncating (+SMAD4 deep del). Sensitivity: score-derived MSS, exclude TMB>20/POLE, include early stage. Label rule: True if KRAS/BRAF/PIK3CA (main) right-enriched with FDR significance and most genes right-direction with none significantly left; False if main genes not right-enriched or significant opposite direction.

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: The web does not settle a cBioPortal convention for CDX. cBioPortal defines SAMPLE_CLASS only loosely as 'the type of sample', it is free text, and there is no standard CDX value (GENIE, for example, uses Tumor/cfDNA). What the literature does establish is that CDX (circulating-tumour-cell-derived xenografts or explants) are grown in mice from CTCs isolated from a patient blood draw (about 10 mL) and are treated as a kind of patient-derived model. So a PDX-class sample whose procedure or source is 'Blood Draw' is most plausibly a CDX, while PDX models from biopsies or resections are tissue-derived. This is an inference, not a documented standard: confirm it in the study's own column descriptions (the # header lines). Even if the CDX are identified, the given tables hold no ASCL1/NEUROD1/POU2F3 expression or subtype variable. QUESTION: In cBioPortal-style clinical files, how are CDX usually recorded; are they coded as SAMPLE_CLASS PDX with procedure 'Blood Draw'? SOURCE: https://groups.google.com/g/cbioportal/c/dTU5QKXT24E ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5583071/ ; https://www.nature.com/articles/s43018-019-0020-z

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In public cancer genomics portal sample tables for patient-derived organoid studies, does the 'therapy prior to derivation' field ever record treatment of the derived model in vivo, or only treatment of the patient before tissue collection? ANSWER: By the conventions I could read, the field records only the patient's treatment before tissue collection, not in vivo treatment of the derived model. Cell Model Passports keeps 'Sample Treatment (Prior Treatment)', defined as any therapy the patient received before sampling, separate from 'Model Treatment', defined as treatment during or after model derivation. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In cBioPortal-style clinical files, how are circulating-tumour-cell-derived xenografts (CDX) usually recorded? Are they coded as SAMPLE_CLASS PDX with procedure 'Blood Draw'? ANSWER: The web does not document a standard cBioPortal convention for CDX. cBioPortal describes SAMPLE_CLASS only loosely as 'the type of sample'; values are free text set by each study (AACR GENIE, for example, uses Tumor/cfDNA), and there is no dedicated CDX value. The literature does establish that CDX models are xenografts or explants grown in immunocompromised mice from circulating tumour cells isolated from a patient blood draw (about 10 mL), as opposed to tissue biopsies. CDX are treated as a type of patient-derived model. So a sample with SAMPLE_CLASS=PDX and procedure or source 'Blood Draw' is most plausibly a CDX, and PDX from biopsy or resection procedures are tissue-derived PDX. This is a reasonable inference, not a documented standard; teams should confirm it from the study's own column descriptions. Even with CDX identified, the subtype question needs ASCL1/NEUROD1/POU2F3 expression or a subtype annotation, which the given tables appear to lack. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://groups.google.com/g/cbioportal/c/dTU5QKXT24E, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5583071/, https://www.nature.com/articles/s43018-019-0020-z, https://docs.cbioportal.org/file-formats/.

RNA_support=Yes with DNA_support=No means the fusion was detected from RNA-seq only and not confirmed in DNA, so RNA-seq existed for that sample even though no expression table was supplied. The definition appears in the same words in several cBioPortal-derived format docs, but the fetched pages were cut off before the SV section, so I saw it only in search excerpts. HOW SURE: medium. QUESTION: Is there published functional evidence on whether ARAF missense variants near the CR2 regulatory region (around residues 214-217) or at the start of the kinase domain (around residue 322) increase MEK/ERK signalling, and what assays are used to show it? ANSWER: Yes for S214 (S214C/F/P) at the CR2 14-3-3 site. Cells engineered to express S214C activate Raf-MEK-ERK signalling (phospho-MEK/ERK immunoblots) and show more proliferation, colony and spheroid formation, migration and invasion, with RNA-seq and RPPA readouts and sorafenib sensitivity. S214P is gain-of-function and treatable with a MEK inhibitor. Kinase-region beta3-alphaC deletions (Q347A348del) activate MEK-ERK in 293T cells. I found no functional evidence or established activating annotation for N217I or G322S. Activation is shown with functional assays, not from genomic calls alone. The absence for N217/G322 rests on limited searching. HOW SURE: medium. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Are fusions of a gene with immunoglobulin lambda segments (IGLJ/IGLL5), detected only from RNA-seq in solid tumours, a known artefact pattern in fusion-calling pipelines? ANSWER: Not settled by the pages I read. Reviews say RNA-only fusion calls carry many false positives from mismapping, homologous or polymorphic regions, very high expression and library artefacts such as template switching. They also say IG loci map poorly and that recurrent immunoglobulin-rearrangement events should be flagged and deprioritised. In a solid tumour, IG-lambda partners plausibly come from infiltrating plasma cells with high IG expression, so these fusions are suspect and weak pathway evidence at best. I found no source naming IGLJ/IGLL5 fusions specifically as a documented artefact. HOW SURE: low. label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Published paired pre/post-trastuzumab gastroesophageal studies (Pietrantonio 2016, n=22 pairs, 32% HER2 loss; GASTHER3 2018, n=48, 29.1% loss) do not use a concurrent untreated control arm. They judge association by comparing the post-progression loss rate with the known background primary-vs-metastasis discordance rate, which is low (about 0.4-7%, and negative conversion is rarer). They also use strict clinical criteria for acquired resistance (benefit followed by progression), and they check heterogeneity directly: GASTHER3 found ISH-defined HER2 genetic heterogeneity in 2.9% of baseline vs 21.9% of post-progression samples, and the loss was linked to poor response to second-line T-DM1. Analysts usually infer selection of a pre-existing HER2-negative subclone when baseline heterogeneity is followed by a HER2-negative post-progression tumour. A loss rate several times above the background discordance rate is taken as treatment-associated, even without a formal control. QUESTION: How do paired pre/post studies decide that biomarker loss is associated with acquired resistance rather than with heterogeneity or assay discordance, and what comparators are used? SOURCE: https://doi.org/10.1002/ijc.30408 ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30386954/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5466678/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: Background HER2 discordance in untreated gastroesophageal cancer is low. Meta-analysis (2017, Sci Rep/PMC5466678): pooled primary-vs-metastasis discordance is 7% (95% CI 5-10%) with the strict IHC3+ or IHC2+/ISH+ definition, versus 12.2% with broad definitions. Kim et al. (FISH): 7/250 (2.8%) paired primary/metastasis cases were discordant, and only 1/250 (0.4%) was a negative conversion (amplified primary, non-amplified metastasis). 6 of the 7 discordant cases showed heterogeneous amplification in the primary. Intratumoural heterogeneous amplification was seen in 8/325 primaries (2.5%), against 8.3% homogeneous amplification, i.e. about 23% of amplified tumours were heterogeneous on three-region sampling. Review ranges are 1-14%. By contrast, post-trastuzumab HER2 loss is about 29-69%, well above this background. QUESTION: What is the background rate of ERBB2/HER2 amplification discordance between synchronous primary and metastatic samples, or across regions of an untreated gastroesophageal tumour? SOURCE: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5466678/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3267049/ ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30386954/

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: In the TCGA BRAF/RAS/NF1/Triple-WT classification, the Triple-WT KIT alterations are listed in Table 1 as 'KIT COSMIC mut/amp', meaning recurrent known (COSMIC/hotspot, activating) KIT mutations, not any non-silent KIT variant. KIT amplification (4q12 focal amplification, often with PDGFRA and KDR) was called from SNP-array copy-number data (GISTIC focal peaks; the TCGA slides used segmented log2 value >0.5 with Fisher tests by subtype). So the amplification half of the claim needs copy-number data, and mutation tables cannot stand in for it. Confidence: medium-high; the Table 1 and 4q12 wording was seen in search snippets of the TCGA paper because the full-text fetch was truncated. QUESTION: Which KIT alterations count as KIT mutations in the melanoma genomic classification, and is KIT amplification reported from copy-number data? label: FINDING
text: FINDING: No published method infers chromoplexy from copy-number segments alone; ChainFinder builds a graph whose nodes are rearrangement junction breakpoints from paired-end WGS and uses deletion segments only as edges ('chromosomal deletions reveal additional chains'), and chromoplexy typically leaves little or no copy-number change (balanced), which arrays/seg data cannot see. CN-only criteria exist for chromothripsis (clustered oscillations between 2-3 CN states on SNP arrays), but they underestimate it and the field moved to SV-based criteria; they do not apply to unclustered multi-chromosome chromoplexy. Seg data are at most a weak, non-diagnostic proxy. QUESTION: Can CN segmentation alone infer or support chromoplexy? SOURCE: https://www.genome.gov/Multimedia/Slides/HGP10Symposium/11_Garraway.pdf ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3673705/ ; https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/8/3826 ; https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-019-0576-7.pdf ; https://genesdev.cshlp.org/content/27/23/2513.full

text: FINDING: PathScan's null explicitly accounts for gene length (longer genes have higher mutation probability under random mutation), computes a per-sample probability that the pathway is hit given that sample's mutation burden, and combines samples with Fisher-Lancaster; MutSigCV likewise defines significance as mutated more often than expected by chance given a background rate and per-gene/per-sample covered bases (assuming full coverage if no coverage file). So the background universe should be all sequenced genes (the whole exome, using CDS length as coverage), not only the genes that happen to appear in a filtered MAF; restricting the universe to MAF genes inflates the pathway's share and makes p swing. An unweighted random gene-set null ignores length and per-sample burden and is the less valid test; prefer the length-weighted per-sample null. The web does not give a recipe for a filtered MAF specifically; that part is inference from the method definitions. QUESTION: background gene universe and length handling; length-weighted per-sample vs unweighted gene-set null. QUESTION: In the genomic classification of cutaneous melanoma into BRAF, RAS, NF1 and triple-wild-type subtypes, which KIT alterations (activating hotspots versus any non-silent mutation) are usually counted as KIT mutations, and is KIT amplification usually reported from copy-number data? KIT amplification is reported from copy-number data: SNP6 array segments analysed by GISTIC, which found a significant 4q12 focal amplification containing KIT only in Triple-WT, often co-amplified with PDGFRA and KDR. The TCGA presentation slides tabulate the percentage of each subtype with KIT amplification, defined as a segmented value above 0.5, with Fisher p=0.00114 and FDR 0.14. Without a copy-number/CNA table, the amplification part of the claim cannot be tested, and mutation calls or ploidy are not a valid substitute. Caveat: the Table 1 and 4q12 wording was read in search-result excerpts of the TCGA paper because the full-text fetches were truncated. The abstract (opened) and the slides (opened) confirm the 'KIT mutations and focal amplifications' claim and that amplification was called from copy number. HOW SURE: medium. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In paired pre/post-treatment tumour genomics studies, how do analysts decide that a change in a biomarker (e.g. loss of a gene amplification) is 'associated with' acquired drug resistance rather than explained by spatial heterogeneity or assay discordance? What comparators or background discordance rates are usually used? ANSWER: The key paired studies in HER2-positive gastroesophageal cancer do not use a concurrent untreated control arm. Pietrantonio et al. 2016 (22 pairs, 32% loss of HER2 positivity) and GASTHER3 2018 (48 pairs, 29.1% loss) instead (1) apply strict clinical criteria for acquired resistance (initial benefit, then progression on trastuzumab, with the biopsy taken after progression); (2) use a strict, prespecified definition of HER2 status (IHC3+ or IHC2+/ISH+) at both time points; (3) compare the loss rate implicitly with the known background primary-vs-metastasis discordance in untreated disease, which is about 0.4-7% overall and lower for negative conversion; and (4) look for heterogeneity directly. GASTHER3 found ISH-defined HER2 genetic heterogeneity in 2.9% of baseline vs 21.9% of post-progression samples, and loss predicted no response to second-line T-DM1. They read a pre-existing heterogeneous or focal amplification followed by a HER2-negative post-progression tumour as selection of an ERBB2-non-amplified subclone. A loss rate several times above background is taken as treatment-associated. Formal tests such as McNemar's test or a control cohort are recommended but rarely used. The web does not show a single formal standard comparator. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://doi.org/10.1002/ijc.30408, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30386954/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5466678/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: What is the reported rate of discordance in ERBB2/HER2 amplification status between synchronous primary and metastatic samples, or between multiple regions of the same untreated gastroesophageal tumour? ANSWER: Background discordance is low. A 2017 meta-analysis gives pooled primary-vs-metastasis discordance of 7% (95% CI 5-10%) with the strict definition (6.2% vs 12.2% for strict vs broad definitions). Kim et al. (FISH, 250 paired primary/metastasis cases, synchronous and metachronous) found 2.8% discordant. Only 0.4% (1/250) were negative conversions (amplified primary, non-amplified metastasis) and 2.4% were positive conversions; 6 of the 7 discordant cases had heterogeneous amplification in the primary. Across three regions of 325 untreated primaries, 2.5% showed heterogeneous amplification against 8.3% homogeneous, so roughly a quarter of amplified tumours were regionally heterogeneous. Reviews quote a 1-14% range. Post-trastuzumab loss rates (29-69%) are far above this sampling background. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5466678/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3267049/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30386954/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In prostate cancer genomics, how is the TMPRSS2-ERG fusion mechanism (interstitial deletion versus balanced translocation) related to chained rearrangements such as chromoplexy, and can FISH 'translocation with deletion' patterns or copy-number deletions at 21q22 be used as evidence of chromoplexy? ANSWER: TMPRSS2-ERG forms either by intrachromosomal deletion of the ~3 Mb region between the genes (the FISH deletion/'Edel' pattern, also visible as a 21q22 CN loss) or by insertion/balanced rearrangement without loss. Both kinds can be part of chromoplexy chains. Baca et al. 2013 found ERG disrupted by chromoplexy in 15 of 26 fusion-positive tumours, and chained rearrangements can carry large 'deletion bridges' at their junctions. None of the sources I read accept a FISH deletion flag or a seg-level 21q22 deletion by itself as evidence of chromoplexy. Calling a chain needs the junction breakpoints that link the deletion to rearrangements on other chromosomes. These variables record how the fusion formed and whether it is present, not whether it arose in a chain. They do not let you test interdependent genesis. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3673705/, https://www.genome.gov/Multimedia/Slides/HGP10Symposium/11_Garraway.pdf, https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/66/17/8337/526226/TMPRSS2-ERG-Fusion-Associated-Deletions-Provide, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4873435/, https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/8/3826.

QUESTION: In prostate cancer genomics, how is the TMPRSS2-ERG fusion mechanism (interstitial deletion versus balanced translocation) related to chained rearrangements such as chromoplexy, and can FISH 'translocation with deletion' patterns or copy-number deletions at 21q22 be used as evidence of chromoplexy? ANSWER: TMPRSS2-ERG forms either by intrachromosomal deletion of the ~3 Mb region between the genes (the FISH deletion/'Edel' pattern, also visible as a 21q22 CN loss) or by insertion/balanced rearrangement without loss. Both kinds can be part of chromoplexy chains. Baca et al. 2013 found ERG disrupted by chromoplexy in 15 of 26 fusion-positive tumours, and chained rearrangements can carry large 'deletion bridges' at their junctions. None of the sources I read accept a FISH deletion flag or a seg-level 21q22 deletion by itself as evidence of chromoplexy. Calling a chain needs the junction breakpoints that link the deletion to rearrangements on other chromosomes. These variables record how the fusion formed and whether it is present, not whether it arose in a chain. They do not let you test interdependent genesis. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3673705/, https://www.genome.gov/Multimedia/Slides/HGP10Symposium/11_Garraway.pdf, https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article/66/17/8337/526226/TMPRSS2-ERG-Fusion-Associated-Deletions-Provide, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4873435/, https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/8/3826.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Can copy-number segmentation data alone (breakpoint positions and segment means, without junction adjacency) be used to infer or support chained rearrangements such as chromoplexy, and what are the published methods or limitations for doing so? ANSWER: No. I found no published method that infers chromoplexy from CN segments alone. ChainFinder (Baca 2013) builds a graph whose nodes are rearrangement breakpoints from paired-end WGS. It uses CN deletion segments only as extra edges between those junctions, and then tests whether connected breakpoints are unlikely to have arisen independently. Chromoplexy is described as producing derivative chromosomes with little or no copy-number change, so much of it is invisible to array or seg data. CN-only operational criteria (clustered oscillations between 2-3 CN states in SNP-array data) exist for chromothripsis, not chromoplexy. Even for chromothripsis they underestimate frequency, and the field has moved to SV- and paired-end-based criteria. Seg breakpoints are therefore at best a weak, non-diagnostic proxy and cannot establish interdependence. The web did not show any accepted CN-only chromoplexy signature. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.genome.gov/Multimedia/Slides/HGP10Symposium/11_Garraway.pdf, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3673705/, https://www.mdpi.com/1422-0067/26/8/3826, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-019-0576-7.pdf, https://genesdev.cshlp.org/content/27/23/2513.full.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In pathway-level significance tests for somatic mutations (e.g. PathScan, MutSig-style or gene-set permutation approaches), how should the background gene universe and gene-length/coverage be handled when the mutation file contains only a filtered subset of genes, and how do the results differ between a length-weighted per-sample null and an unweighted random gene-set null? ANSWER: PathScan's null is built on gene length: under random mutation, longer genes are more likely to be hit. It computes a per-sample probability that the pathway is mutated given that sample's mutation burden, then combines samples using Fisher-Lancaster. MutSigCV also defines significance against a background rate per covered base, per gene and per patient, and assumes full coverage when no coverage file is given. The background universe should therefore be all sequenced genes, i.e. the whole exome weighted by CDS length, not only the genes that appear in a filtered MAF. Shrinking the universe to MAF genes inflates the pathway's share and makes the p-value unstable. An unweighted random gene-set null ignores both gene length and per-sample burden, so the length-weighted per-sample (PathScan-style) null is the valid choice. No source gives a recipe for a filtered MAF; that part is my inference from how the methods are defined. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3106187/, https://www.genepattern.org/modules/docs/MutSigCV/1/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3919509/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In standard curated pathway definitions (e.g. TCGA 2018 oncogenic signaling pathways, KEGG ErbB), are RAS genes (KRAS/HRAS/NRAS) considered part of the 'ERBB-PI3K' signaling pathway or a separate RTK-RAS pathway? ANSWER: The TCGA 2018 curation (Sanchez-Vega et al.) treats PI3K/Akt and RTK-RAS as two separate pathways. KRAS, NRAS and HRAS belong to RTK-RAS, together with EGFR, ERBB2-4, BRAF and NF1. KEGG hsa04012 (ErbB signaling) does include a RAS-ERK branch (element N00021, EGF-ERBB2-RAS-ERK) alongside its PI3K branch. A label like 'ERBB-PI3K' most naturally means the ERBB receptors plus the PI3K axis, without RAS. Including RAS follows the broader KEGG ErbB convention. Run both as a sensitivity check. The truncated page text did not show the full gene tables, so the RAS placement in TCGA rests on the figure text and the pathway list. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6070353/, https://iris.uniroma1.it/bitstream/11573/1762329/1/Sanchez-Vega_Oncogenic-Signaling-Pathways_2018.pdf, https://www.kegg.jp/entry/hsa04012.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Does the presence of known activating hotspot mutations in a few samples constitute evidence that a pathway is 'significantly mutated' in the statistical sense used by cancer-genomics studies, or is that term reserved for a frequency-versus-background test? ANSWER: In cancer genomics, 'significantly mutated' is a statistical term. It means a gene or pathway is mutated more often than chance would predict under a background mutation model (as in MutSigCV and PathScan), with FDR control. Known hotspots in a few samples show functional or driver relevance, which is how TCGA 2018 counts OncoKB-curated alterations, but they are not on their own evidence of statistical significance. Hotspot or clustering evidence counts only when it is part of a test against a background. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://www.genepattern.org/modules/docs/MutSigCV/1/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3919509/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3106187/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6070353/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: When somatic variants are called from a tumour without a matched normal and from a related sample with a matched normal, what fraction of tumour-only calls is typically germline, and what filters are standard for removing them? ANSWER: A large share can be germline. A Cancer Discovery news summary of a Johns Hopkins study of 815 tumour/normal pairs reported that 249 of 382 candidate somatic alterations from tumour-only analysis (about 65%) proved to be germline. The usual filters are: remove sites found in population databases (dbSNP, 1000 Genomes, ExAC/gnomAD) above a population-frequency cutoff, commonly 1-2%, which McNulty 2019 shows should be tuned per assay; use a germline resource with a population-frequency prior plus a panel of normals (Mutect2 --germline-resource and --panel-of-normals); flag variant allele fractions near 50% or 100%; and compare against unmatched normals (UNMASC). Rare private germline variants survive database filters, so tumour-only calls stay noisier than matched calls even after filtering. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://aacrjournals.org/cancerdiscovery/article/5/7/OF17/5149/Tumor-Only-Sequencing-Has-LimitationsTumor-Only, https://www.jmdjournal.org/article/S1525-1578(19)30084-4/fulltext, https://gatk.broadinstitute.org/hc/en-us/articles/360036490432-Mutect2, https://digitalcommons.wustl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2800&context=oa_4.

QUESTION: When comparing a 3-level categorical risk score against a 6-level ordinal clinical index for survival prediction, what is the accepted way to handle tied predictions in Harrell's C, and is comparing against a collapsed version of the index considered a fair like-for-like comparison? It is best treated as a sensitivity analysis next to the comparison against the full IPI as used in the clinic, not as a replacement for it. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In patient-derived xenograft studies, how is clonal selection at engraftment usually told apart from spatial sampling heterogeneity and passage drift, for example with replicate tumour pieces or clonal prevalence estimates? ANSWER: The studies I read used multi-region sampling of the patient tumour and several independent PDX models from different regions. TRACERx lung PDX (Nat Commun 2024) found a genomic bottleneck at establishment, with models often representing a single subclone. Different regions gave different subclones, and evolution in mice added only modestly to the tumour-PDX distance. Woo 2021 (Nat Genet) used multi-region variation within a patient as the baseline: patient-PDX CNA differences were comparable to that variation, with no systematic evolution. Serial-passage multiregion designs (Cancer Genomics Proteomics 2019) track subclone prevalence across passages to separate drift. Selection is inferred when the change from tumour to first xenograft is larger than the variation between regions or replicates, and when pre-existing minor subclones become dominant. I read mostly abstracts, so method details are limited. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-47547-3, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41588-020-00750-6, https://cgp.iiarjournals.org/content/16/1/21.

QUESTION: In prognostic model validation, when Harrell's C and AIC/likelihood ratio disagree about which of two non-nested models is better, which is conventionally used to claim one model 'outperforms' another, and how should in-sample derivation of one model affect AIC comparisons? ANSWER: The two sources point different ways. The methodological view (Harrell) is that likelihood-based measures (LR chi-square, AIC) are the gold standard and that comparing two c-indexes is a low-power method. For non-nested models he recommends fitting the combined model and running LR tests of the combined model against each single model (the adequacy index), or a head-to-head paired concordance comparison such as Hmisc rcorrp.cens. Applied prognostic papers, though, usually claim 'outperforms' on discrimination: a higher C with a paired test or CI. If C and AIC disagree, neither convention clearly supports 'outperforms', and the claim should be called unsettled or weak, not proven. AIC penalises only the number of estimated parameters. It does not correct for choosing variables or cut-points from the same data, so a genomic model derived on this cohort has optimistic apparent AIC and C, while IPI was fixed externally. Steyerberg recommends bootstrap internal validation that repeats every modelling step. An in-sample advantage for the derived model is therefore weaker evidence, and an in-sample advantage for the external index is stronger evidence. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.fharrell.com/post/addvalue/, https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/561464/anova-model-comparison-versus-concordance-index-comparison-in-deciding-best-mode, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1712.02379, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5578404/.

QUESTION: In prognostic model validation, when Harrell's C and AIC/likelihood ratio disagree about which of two non-nested models is better, which is conventionally used to claim one model 'outperforms' another, and how should in-sample derivation of one model affect AIC comparisons? ANSWER: The two sources point different ways. The methodological view (Harrell) is that likelihood-based measures (LR chi-square, AIC) are the gold standard and that comparing two c-indexes is a low-power method. For non-nested models he recommends fitting the combined model and running LR tests of the combined model against each single model (the adequacy index), or a head-to-head paired concordance comparison such as Hmisc rcorrp.cens. Applied prognostic papers, though, usually claim 'outperforms' on discrimination: a higher C with a paired test or CI. If C and AIC disagree, neither convention clearly supports 'outperforms', and the claim should be called unsettled or weak, not proven. AIC penalises only the number of estimated parameters. It does not correct for choosing variables or cut-points from the same data, so a genomic model derived on this cohort has optimistic apparent AIC and C, while IPI was fixed externally. Steyerberg recommends bootstrap internal validation that repeats every modelling step. An in-sample advantage for the derived model is therefore weaker evidence, and an in-sample advantage for the external index is stronger evidence. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://www.fharrell.com/post/addvalue/, https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/561464/anova-model-comparison-versus-concordance-index-comparison-in-deciding-best-mode, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1712.02379, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5578404/.

text: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How do tumour purity and ploidy differences distort comparisons of log2 copy-number ratios between two samples, and can linear rescaling remove the effect? ANSWER: Observed copy ratio = (p*n + 2(1-p)) / (average ploidy of the mixture), where p is purity and n is copy number. For example, CNVkit notes that a single-copy loss at 50% purity gives log2(0.75) = -0.415 rather than -1. Lower purity compresses log2 values towards 0, and the compression is non-linear in log2 space, so one multiplier on log2 values does not undo it exactly. The correction is linear in ratio space, not log space. CNVkit's call --purity rescales on that basis, but it assumes a known purity, a fixed reference ploidy and clonal events. Ploidy differences between samples shift where the neutral baseline sits after centring, and subclonal events break the integer model. Linear rescaling therefore removes purity effects only roughly. Ploidy and subclonality need a joint purity/ploidy fit (e.g. PureCN, THetA2) or comparison of discretised gain/loss calls and breakpoints. The formula is the standard mixture model shown in CNVkit's docs; the source text cut off before the function implementing it. HOW SURE: medium. SOURCES: https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/latest/heterogeneity.html, https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/calling.html, https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/_modules/cnvlib/call.html.

FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: What methods are recommended for comparing the discrimination of two survival predictors when the proportional hazards assumption is violated (e.g. Uno's IPCW C, time-dependent AUC at fixed horizons), and what are their defaults in common R packages? ANSWER: Under non-PH, use truncated Uno IPCW C and/or IPCW cumulative/dynamic time-dependent AUC at fixed horizons (for example 2 and 5 years). These are rank measures and do not depend on a single hazard ratio. Defaults in the R docs I read:

- **survival::concordance** gives Harrell's C by default (timewt='n'). timewt='n/G2' gives Uno's C, and ymax= restricts the time range to tau. Passing several fits, as in concordance(fit1, fit2), gives an infinitesimal-jackknife covariance that is valid even for non-nested models, but the rows must line up exactly (watch for missing values).
- **survC1::Est.Cval(mydata, tau, nofit=FALSE)** has no default tau; the user must set it, and the censoring survival must be positive at tau. Inf.Cval.Delta(mydata, covs0, covs1, tau, itr=1000) tests the Uno C difference by resampling.
- **timeROC::timeROC(T, delta, marker, cause, weighting='marginal', times, ROC=TRUE, iid=FALSE)** uses Kaplan-Meier censoring weights by default. iid=TRUE is needed for confidence intervals and for testing two markers measured on the same subjects; the companion compare() function was not on the page I read. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/survival/html/concordance.html, https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/survC1/html/Est.Cval.html, https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/survC1/html/Inf.Cval.Delta.html, https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/timeROC/html/timeROC.html.

text: FINDING: VEP assigns consequences per transcript; upstream_gene_variant means the variant lies outside that transcript, within 5 kb (default --distance) upstream of its 5' end, while missense_variant on the canonical transcript means it sits in the canonical coding sequence. Together these place the variant inside the gene body (a coding exon of the canonical isoform), upstream of an alternative isoform whose TSS lies further downstream. vcf2maf and gene-level reporting use the canonical/most severe call (Missense_Mutation), so by convention it is a coding mutation, not a promoter mutation; at most it could sit in an alternative-isoform promoter region, which needs separate evidence. QUESTION: Does an alternative-transcript upstream_gene_variant plus canonical missense_variant count as a promoter variant? SOURCE: https://useast.ensembl.org/info/genome/variation/prediction/predicted_data.html

label: FINDING
text: FINDING: The web pages read did not settle one convention. Cancer non-coding studies define promoters as windows around annotated TSSs, e.g. +/-500 bp (Fredriksson 2017 melanoma, PLoS Genet), -1000/+500 bp on canonical transcripts (Abad 2024 bioRxiv, PCAWG data), +/-200 bp around each transcript TSS (PCAWG, search snippet only) and -2000/+200 bp (BJC 2024, snippet only). Downstream windows can overlap the 5'UTR and sometimes the first coding bases. However, PCAWG keeps CDS, 5'UTR and promoter as separate element classes, and recurrent promoter mutations reported in melanoma are non-coding TSS-proximal sites (e.g. TERT, ETS/TTCCG motifs). A missense hotspot in a coding exon is normally reported as a coding mutation, not a promoter mutation. Confidence is low to medium. QUESTION: How do cancer genomics papers define the promoter region for recurrent promoter mutations? SOURCE: https://journals.plos.org/plosgenetics/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pgen.1006773 ; https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.06.03.597231v1.full ; http://pcawg.gersteinlab.org/ ; https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/237313v1.supplementary-material

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: How can tumour purity or cellularity be estimated for an exome-sequenced sample when only segmented log2 copy-ratio values and a mutation list without read counts are available, and how strongly does low purity attenuate log2 ratios toward zero for single-copy gains and losses? ANSWER: For a diploid genome with purity p and a clonal event, the expected log2 ratio is log2((p*CN + 2(1-p))/2). CNVkit's docs give the 50% case: a single-copy loss is log2(0.75) = -0.415. A single-copy loss is -1.0 at 100% purity, -0.415 at 50%, -0.234 at 30%, -0.152 at 20% and -0.074 at 10%. A single-copy gain is +0.585 at 100%, +0.322 at 50%, +0.202 at 30%, +0.138 at 20% and +0.070 at 10%. At 30% purity, single-copy events sit right at the common 0.2/-0.25 cutoffs; at 20% or below they fall under them. Without read counts or VAFs, the only data-based way to estimate purity is to fit the observed segment log2 levels to the expected levels for integer copy states (CNVkit's approach 4; PureCN and ABSOLUTE fit purity and ploidy jointly). This is unreliable when a sample has few events. Other options are a pathologist's estimate, or VAFs of clonal mutations and BAF shifts, which need read counts. A near-zero JP profile fits purity of about 10-20%, but from log2 alone you cannot tell dilution apart from a genuinely quiet genome. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/heterogeneity.html, https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/calling.html, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9302205/, https://www.keatslab.org/blog/dnacopynumberanditseffectsonlog2valuesandallelicratiosatdifferenttumorpurities.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In copy-number studies comparing precursor and invasive breast lesions, is 'number of copy number alterations' usually reported as a count of discrete events (after merging segments) or as fraction of genome altered, and how are low-amplitude segments in exome-derived copy-number data usually treated? ANSWER: There is no single convention, and the pages I read do not fully settle it. Precursor-lesion papers describe burden as numbers of discrete aberrations: 'ADH ... had fewer aberrations than LG or HG DCIS', and '18 copy number changes' across 9 ADHs. Matched DCIS/IDC studies often use fraction of genome altered or shared. cBioPortal's FGA is the length of segments with |log2| > 0.1 divided by the genome length (another post says 0.2), weighted by bases, not by segment count. Low-amplitude segments are treated as copy-neutral below a fixed |log2| cutoff, typically 0.1-0.3; CNVkit's defaults are -0.25 and +0.2. Results are known to depend on the cutoff. None of the methods sections I read describe how segments are merged into events. If the counts are equal while FGA differs, report the result as metric-dependent. Neither metric gives JP 'more' CNAs. HOW SURE: low. SOURCES: https://pathsocjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/path.5262, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3346166/, https://www.biostars.org/p/406584/, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41698-023-00408-6, https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/calling.html.

QUESTION: In copy-number studies comparing precursor and invasive breast lesions, is 'number of copy number alterations' usually reported as a count of discrete events (after merging segments) or as fraction of genome altered, and how are low-amplitude segments in exome-derived copy-number data usually treated? ANSWER: There is no single convention, and the pages I read do not fully settle it. Precursor-lesion papers describe burden as numbers of discrete aberrations: 'ADH ... had fewer aberrations than LG or HG DCIS', and '18 copy number changes' across 9 ADHs. Matched DCIS/IDC studies often use fraction of genome altered or shared. cBioPortal's FGA is the length of segments with |log2| > 0.1 divided by the genome length (another post says 0.2), weighted by bases, not by segment count. Low-amplitude segments are treated as copy-neutral below a fixed |log2| cutoff, typically 0.1-0.3; CNVkit's defaults are -0.25 and +0.2. Results are known to depend on the cutoff. None of the methods sections I read describe how segments are merged into events. If the counts are equal while FGA differs, report the result as metric-dependent. Neither metric gives JP 'more' CNAs. HOW SURE: low. SOURCES: https://pathsocjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/path.5262, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3346166/, https://www.biostars.org/p/406584/, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41698-023-00408-6, https://cnvkit.readthedocs.io/en/stable/calling.html.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In Ensembl VEP, when a variant is annotated upstream_gene_variant for one transcript of a gene but missense_variant for that gene's canonical transcript, what does that imply about the variant's position? Is it conventionally treated as a promoter variant? ANSWER: VEP predicts consequences separately for each transcript. upstream_gene_variant means the variant lies outside that transcript, within 5 kb (the default --distance) upstream of its 5' end. missense_variant on the canonical transcript means the variant is inside the canonical coding sequence. Together, the variant sits in a coding exon in the gene body of the canonical isoform, upstream of an alternative isoform whose transcription start is further downstream. Gene-level reporting (vcf2maf/MAF Variant_Classification) uses the canonical or most severe consequence, so the variant is conventionally a coding missense mutation, not a promoter mutation. An alternative-transcript upstream tag alone does not make it a promoter variant. At most it might fall in an alternative-isoform promoter, which would need separate evidence such as a TSS-relative distance or a regulatory annotation. (The positional reading is documented; the coding-not-promoter convention is inferred from standard VEP/MAF practice.) HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://useast.ensembl.org/info/genome/variation/prediction/predicted_data.html.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In cancer genomics papers that report recurrent 'promoter mutations' of a gene found by exome or whole-genome sequencing, how is the promoter region usually defined: distance from the canonical TSS, inclusion of 5'UTR, or inclusion of sites within the first coding exon? ANSWER: The pages I read did not settle a single convention. Promoters are usually defined as a window around annotated TSSs, not by UTR or exon status. Examples: +/-500 bp around TSSs (Fredriksson et al. 2017, melanoma); -1000/+500 bp on canonical transcripts (Abad et al. 2024 bioRxiv, which calls this more inclusive than earlier studies); +/-200 bp around each transcript's TSS (PCAWG; seen only in a search snippet); -2000/+200 bp (BJC 2024; snippet only). The downstream part of these windows can overlap the 5'UTR and, where the start codon is close to the TSS, a few first-exon coding bases. PCAWG, however, annotates CDS, 5'UTR and promoter as separate element classes. The recurrent melanoma promoter mutations described are non-coding, TSS-proximal sites (TERT; ETS/TTCCG motifs). A missense hotspot inside a coding exon would normally be reported as a coding mutation, not a promoter mutation. Whether first-exon coding sites count as 'promoter' is not settled by the web pages read. HOW SURE: low. SOURCES: https://journals.plos.org/plosgenetics/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pgen.1006773, https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2024.06.03.597231v1.full, http://pcawg.gersteinlab.org/, https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/237313v1.supplementary-material, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4217527/.

text: FINDING: The most common sidedness convention puts the whole transverse colon on the right (cecum through transverse colon = right; splenic flexure through rectum = left). The embryology-based version splits the transverse colon: the proximal two-thirds (midgut) is right and the distal third (hindgut) is left. Some large analyses (ARCAD, GISCAD) leave transverse colon out or treat it as its own group, and Loree et al. found transverse tumours cluster more like left-sided ones. A provided label that splits the transverse colon therefore follows a recognised convention but not the most common one, so a sensitivity analysis (transverse all right, or transverse excluded) is advisable. Rectum is usually grouped with left-sided disease in mCRC sidedness work, but many studies also analyse it separately (Caris: left colon vs right colon vs rectum); Loree found the sigmoid-rectal region distinct. QUESTION: In clonal-evolution studies of paired tumour samples, is 'acquired alterations' usually counted per patient, per sample pair, or per unit time? How are patients with different numbers of samples handled? ANSWER: There is no single standard. A common choice is one comparison per patient, earliest sample against latest. A Foundation Medicine paired-biopsy analysis (Genome Med 2021) kept only the first and last sample for patients with more than two, and grouped results by the time between biopsies. That way each patient adds one value, and patients with more samples don't count for more. Adding up gains over every pair in a patient inflates counts for patients with more samples. If the time between samples differs a lot, report it or divide by the interval. Caveat: this comes from a search snippet; I could not open the full text. HOW SURE: low. question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: In colorectal cancer sidedness studies, how is transverse colon conventionally classified (right, left, or split at a point), and is rectum usually analysed together with left colon or separately? ANSWER: Most common convention: the whole transverse colon counts as right (cecum through transverse colon = right; splenic flexure through rectum = left; the split is at the splenic flexure). The embryology-based alternative splits the transverse colon: the proximal two-thirds (midgut) is right and the distal third (hindgut) is left. Some large analyses (ARCAD, GISCAD) exclude transverse colon or treat it as its own group, and Loree et al. found transverse tumours cluster more like left-sided ones. A label that splits the transverse colon is therefore a recognised but less common choice, and a sensitivity analysis (transverse all right, and/or transverse excluded) is advisable. Rectum is usually grouped with left in mCRC sidedness analyses, but many studies analyse it separately (e.g. Caris: left colon vs right colon vs rectum), and the sigmoid-rectal region differs molecularly (more TP53, less PIK3CA/BRAF), so rectum-excluded sensitivity is also reasonable. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://jgo.amegroups.org/article/view/89938/html, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5844818/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5689690/.

question: FINDING FROM THE LAB'S LIBRARY, asked for by the director. QUESTION: Which RNF43, SMAD4 and BRAF variant classes does OncoKB annotate as oncogenic or likely oncogenic (e.g. RNF43 G659fs, SMAD4 missense, BRAF non-V600 classes)? ANSWER: RNF43: Truncating Mutations (nonsense, frameshift, splice) are Likely Oncogenic, but G659fs*41 has its own Inconclusive call because the functional data conflict. Strict OncoKB annotation therefore excludes G659fs, while a generic 'truncating' rule includes it. SMAD4: Deletion and Truncating Mutations are Likely Oncogenic. About 55 oncogenic or likely oncogenic SMAD4 alterations are listed, mostly specific MH1/MH2 missense changes (e.g. R361C/G/H, D351H/N, D537 variants, R496H, R497H, G386D, C324Y). There are also 1 neutral and 4 inconclusive variants, so only curated SMAD4 missense changes count, not all of them. BRAF: 137 oncogenic alterations, including V600 and many non-V600 class 2/3 variants (G464, G466, G469, N581, D594, L597, K601) and fusions. 44 neutral and 21 inconclusive BRAF variants are also listed, so not every BRAF missense is oncogenic. The page text did not show the per-variant label next to every SMAD4/BRAF entry. HOW SURE: high. SOURCES: https://www.oncokb.org/gene/RNF43, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/RNF43/G659fs*41, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/RNF43/Truncating%20Mutations, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/SMAD4, https://www.oncokb.org/gene/BRAF.
